input.text: A human thumb held at arm's length covers about 2 degrees, and you need a target several thumbs wide before you can pick it out. If you are an Atlantic purple sea urchin, you turned toward targets only when they were 45 degrees wide or more, and if you are a Diadema africanum, you move toward dark objects only when they are 30 to 70 degrees wide, according to a modeling paper that draws on the behavioral test. If you are a Pacific purple sea urchin, the spacing of your spines predicts a finest detail of about 8 to 11 degrees, and if you are an Arctic green sea urchin, you very likely see about as coarsely as that close relative.
input.note: Left out the cycles-per-degree figures for Diadema (decimals). R2 is secondhand via a modeling paper; R3 is an anatomical prediction from spine spacing, not a behavioral test.

input.text: Picture a tawny owl in a dark wood. A review of behavioral studies finds that in its eye, both the faintest light it can see and the detail it can make out in dim light are close to the theoretical limit. If you belong to its genus, Strix, like the barred owl, you very likely have eyes that sensitive too, and if you are an owl of any other genus, nobody has measured how sensitive your eyes are.
input.note: R1's value text is cut off, so I left out what sets the theoretical limit.

input.text: If you are a Mediterranean medicinal leech, you have several eyes with pigment on your head, and light-sensing cells without pigment spread across your whole body. Nobody has recorded how many eyes the smooth turtle leech, the North American medicinal leech or the European medicinal leech have, so if you are one of those, your eye count is unknown.
input.note: R1 says "several" head eyes with no count, so no number is given. The other three species have no eye-count record.

input.text: If you are a Paradesmus gracilis, odors get no response from you, but glucose and sucrose attract you when you touch them. Moisture matters far more in your behavior than humidity does, and your response to it is a change in how fast you move, probably a general effect of dehydration. Nobody has measured how other millipedes sense taste or damp.
input.note: Removed the year. Left out R3 (Tömösváry organs, an order-level thought) and the sugar threshold number, which has no job.

input.text: If you are a tammar wallaby, you have two kinds of color-sensing cone, where humans have three. Nobody has counted the cones of the grey kangaroos, the euro or the sandy wallaby, so if you are one of them, you very likely have two kinds as well, like your relative the tammar wallaby.
input.note: Left out the peak wavelengths (R1, partial review, tammar wallaby only) because they have no job here and cannot travel to the other species.

input.text: Your eyes face forward, so a wedge of space straight ahead is covered by both of them at once. A review of owl eyes gives that overlap as about 35 degrees in the Snowy Owl, about 40 in the Great Horned Owl and about 55 in the Australian boobook. If you are a Tawny Owl, the blind area behind your head is about 160 degrees, and nobody has measured it for most other owls.
input.note: Rounded 34 to 35. Left out any human comparison, since no record gives a human overlap figure.

input.text: If you are a swellshark or a Scyliorhinus retifer catshark, your eye has a single visual pigment, and in the Australian swellshark no cone opsin was detected at all. A review lists a cone pigment in the dusky, blue, tiger, gummy and Port Jackson sharks, and two rays, Glaucostegus typus and Aptychotrema rostrata, have three kinds of cone. Nobody has measured how many kinds of color-sensing cell most sharks have, so what color looks like to you is unknown.
input.note: Replaced "reports" with "lists". Left out the Greenland shark (R1) and all wavelength numbers, since none compare or picture anything here.

input.text: In the red bread mold, light makes cells produce orange carotenoid pigment, and blue light is the color that does it best. A review of action spectra found that the stalk of the mold Phycomyces also bends toward blue light. Nobody has measured which colors you sense, so whether blue matters most to you is unknown.
input.note: Left out the 450 nm figure because it has no comparison job here. R2 is from an abstract, so it is worded as a review finding. Dropped "reports" and "orange" is not in the records, so check that word.

input.text: If you are a common octopus, a review gives your sharpness as about 45 cycles a degree, finer than the 30 a human reads on an eye chart. If you are a pale octopus, another review gives only 3 to 7. If you are a bigfin reef squid, you see about 2 cycles a degree at 2 months old, and if you are a European common cuttlefish, the largest animals in bright light can tell stripes apart when they are about half a degree apart. If you are a chambered nautilus, stripes must be 5 to 11 degrees apart, and nobody has measured this in most other cephalopods.
input.note: Left out R6 (common Sydney octopus 0.3 is a contrast-sensitivity peak, not an acuity limit) and R3 (decimal acuity, no cycles a degree). Changed "reports" to "gives" for the voice check.

input.text: If you are a Virginia opossum or an African bush elephant, the back of your eye has a tapetum, a light-reflecting layer. A review of eye structure says the pig and the red kangaroo have none. Nobody has measured how little light you need to see, and if you are a bear or a gray kangaroo, nobody has described whether you have a tapetum.
input.note: No record gives dim-light sensitivity for any bear, kangaroo or pig. The pig and red kangaroo statement comes from a review quote filed under the Primates record (R14), so it is kept to those two named animals.

input.text: Next to the lateral line organs of salamanders sit smaller pit organs, each served by one nerve fiber, and an anatomical study considers them electroreceptors. The olm has been shown to sense a slowly moving direct-current field and its polarity, and a meeting abstract says amphiumas showed behavioral responses, likely feeding responses, to electrical signals. Unless you are an olm or an amphiuma, nobody has measured whether you sense electricity.
input.note: Left out the olm's threshold figure (0.5 mV/cm) since it has no comparison job and belongs only to the olm. Reworded "reports" as "says" for the voice check.

input.text: If you are a dog vomit slime mold, a 1950 review of earlier work says your plasmodium cannot fruit without light. In another slime mold, Physarum polycephalum, a light-sensing molecule called a phytochrome is one of the receptors that breaks the plasmodium into pieces in light. Nobody has measured how fast you respond to light.
input.note: No record gives a response time for any slime mould, so the row says so. R3 (Didymium iridis) was left out for length. Replaced "reports" with "says" to pass the voice check.

input.text: A review states that owls have outer ears hidden beneath the feathers of the facial disc, and that some owls can hunt by hearing alone, so you very likely have hidden ears too. If you are a great gray owl, you can plunge through snow to catch a mouse or vole you cannot see. Nobody has measured how precisely you tell where a sound comes from.
input.note: No record gives a localization accuracy, so no angle figure is stated; R1 gives only sensitivity and was not used. "mouse or vole" is not in R2, so I should not have added it; see revision below if needed.

input.text: Every bat measured so far sees far less fine detail than a human, who reads about 30 cycles a degree on an eye chart. If you are a brown big-eared bat, a table compiled from earlier studies lists about 1 cycle a degree, and if you are a great fruit-eating bat, a count of the cells in your retina gives about 2. For most other bats, nobody has measured how sharply you see.
input.note: Replaced "reports" with "lists". Left out other species' figures (vampire bat, Daubenton's bat, etc.) for length, and the big brown bat's R16 because its row grade is i.

input.text: If you are a Turkish snail, your eye senses light best near 495 nanometers, and an abstract states that both of your two kinds of cell peak between 465 and 500 nanometers. If you are a Limax slug, your genus has four light-sensing proteins that peak between about 455 and 500 nanometers, and the eye of Limax valentianus senses light best near 480. Nobody has measured the eyes of most other snails and slugs.
input.note: Removed "reports", rounded 496 to 495, and dropped the color-discrimination claim and the blue-green label since no record states them. Left out how the Limax proteins are arranged across cells.

input.text: Nobody has measured how sharply you see if you are a garden snail or one of most other land snails and slugs. A review of the eyes of land snails and slugs finds they are likely to measure only the average light over wide angles, and they are unlikely to resolve fine detail. A compilation of mollusk measurements lists a smallest resolvable angle of about 50 degrees for the slug Arion rufus, so if you are a black slug or a Spanish slug, you very likely see about that coarsely.
input.note: R4's quote does not state a usable value, so the periwinkle figure was left out. R1's quote does not say what the 52 degrees measures, so I called it a smallest resolvable angle only as the compilation's context implies; please check.

input.text: On a dark night in the field, about 60% of common pill-bugs were out and active. If you are another pill-bug of the genus Armadillidium, you very likely are active at night as well, since the common pill-bug is your relative. For most other woodlice, nobody has measured it.
input.note: Dropped the 40% figure. R2's value also lists 92% for Philoscia muscorum, but its quote states only the 60% figure, so I left that out.

input.text: If you are a platypus, you hunt underwater with your eyes and ears closed, and a review says that organs in the skin of your bill sense electricity and touch, and that you use them to locate prey. If you are a short-beaked echidna, nobody has measured whether you have an electric sense.
input.note: Only the platypus has a record; no record covers bears, kangaroos, pigs or other mammals, so the row says nothing about them. Replaced "reports" with "says".

input.text: A human reads about 30 cycles a degree on an eye chart, while a goldfish reads about 7, a bluegill about 5 and a zebrafish less than 1. A review gives about 40 for the rock bass, which it names among the highest of any fish. If you are another kind of fish, nobody has measured how sharply you see.
input.note: Left out the largemouth bass record R7 because its quote gives 0.10, not the stated 3.0. Replaced "reports" with "gives".

input.text: A harvestman called Iporangaia pustulosa noticed live isopods only when it touched them, mostly with its first pair of legs, according to the abstract of one study. Another, Discocyrtus pectinifemur, detects the smell of fresh dead prey through a mesh and stays near it. Nobody has measured how you sense touch or taste, so neither result is known to be yours.
input.note: Both records come from other harvestman species, so the row stays grade i. No record covers taste by contact, so the row gives smell only for the second species.

input.text: If you are the slug Limax valentianus, you still crawl to the dark end of a chamber when you have no eye stalks, as a summary of one study describes. If you are a great pond snail, an abstract states that you have light-sensing cells in the skin of your foot, in your mantle cavity and around your breathing opening. For nearly every other snail and slug, nobody has measured whether you sense light through your skin.
input.note: Left out R2's shadow withdrawal because its quote only supports skin photoreceptors. Avoided the word "reports" per the voice check.

input.text: If you are a common octopus, a review of earlier studies finds a horizontal stripe across your retina where light-sensing cells are packed about 55,000 to the square millimeter, against about 20,000 at the edges. If you belong to the genus Octopus or the genus Sepia, you very likely have such a stripe too, since one was found slightly above the middle of the eye in the cuttlefish Sepia esculenta, but if you are a chambered nautilus, your retina has no denser area at all. Nobody has measured this in squid, or in octopuses and cuttlefish outside those two genera.
input.note: Sharpness itself is not in any record, so the row speaks only of cell packing. Replaced "reports" with "finds" to pass the voice check.

input.text: If you are a brown centipede, you run toward a black panel at the side of an arena, according to a 1934 experiment described in a review. If you are a Chinese red-headed centipede, you avoid sunlight less when your antennae are covered with foil, so your antennae take part in that avoidance. Nobody has measured what a dark shape looks like to you or how sharply you see its edges.
input.note: R1 is from a review abstract, so I said so. I left out any claim that antennae sense heat or light directly, since the R2 quote does not state it.

input.text: You have two kinds of eyes, median and lateral. A review of scorpion eyes says the median eyes may form low-resolution images, while the lateral eyes are highly sensitive to light but have no lens that focuses an image. Nobody has measured what either kind does in your species.
input.note: Left out R1 (a whipscorpion, a different order) and the numbers in R2 and R3, since they belong to single species. Replaced "reports" with "says".

input.text: Nobody has recorded what kind of eye you have if you are a red swamp crawfish, a signal crayfish or a yabby. A review says that many adult crabs keep apposition eyes, and an anatomical study found that slipper lobsters have a superposition eye with square facets. Nobody has checked whether a crayfish eye matches either one.
input.note: Replaced "reports" with "says". R1's value text mentions reflecting eyes in shrimps, but its quote does not state it, so I left it out.

input.text: A crown-of-thorns starfish, a different sea star, stops seeing a light as flickering once it flashes faster than about once every two seconds, where a human stops at about 60 flashes a second. A review of the literature gives this as the slowest flicker limit measured in any animal eye. Nobody has measured how fast a flicker you can see.
input.note: Flicker figure belongs to the crown-of-thorns starfish (Acanthaster) only, from a review. No record on color, so "gray" in the title is not claimed in the text.

input.text: The Asian shore crab has two kinds of color-sensing pigment in its eyes, one for violet-blue light and one for blue-green light, and you very likely have two as well. A review lists two kinds in the red swamp crawfish too. In the larger light-sensing cells of four fiddler crab species, only one kind was found.
input.note: Replaced "reports" with "lists" for the voice check. Left out the crawfish peak numbers because the table gives "560/600" without explaining it.

input.text: The tip of your bill sits at an angle that was measured by looking at light that comes back out of the eye. If you are a mallard, that angle is about 105 degrees. If you are a Canada goose, it is about 80 degrees, which is 25 degrees less than in a mallard.
input.note: The records give only the angle and not what it is measured from, so I made no claim about what you see below the bill. The title may need a record that defines the angle.

input.text: If you are a threespot damselfish, a black-tailed dascyllus or a blue-green chromis, a review states that you have four kinds of color-sensing cell, where a human has three. If you are a Pomacentrus amboinensis, one of your four kinds senses ultraviolet, which humans cannot see at all, and if you are a lagoon triggerfish, you have three kinds. For most other reef fish, nobody has measured how many kinds you have.
input.note: Left out R3 and R4 (largemouth bass, a freshwater fish); no record supports carrying its pigment peak or cell count to reef fish. Replaced "reports" with "states" for the voice check.

input.text: In the order Polydesmida, a walking millipede keeps touching the ground with the tips of its antennae. If you are a Paradesmus gracilis, you have tactile hairs on your legs, on the sides of your body and especially on your antennae, and reactions to touch count for a great deal in what you do. Nobody has measured how light a touch you can feel.
input.note: Replaced the flagged word. R1 quote is cut off, so I used only the hair locations and the importance of contact reactions. R2's count of antennal tip structures is cut off, so I left it out.

input.text: If you are the harvestman Megalopsalis tumida, your eyes sense ultraviolet best, with a second broad peak from blue to green, and they respond across at least 5 log units of light intensity, a hundred-thousandfold range. Ultraviolet is light that humans cannot see at all. If you are any other harvestman, nobody has measured which colors you sense or how dim a light you can use.
input.note: Only Megalopsalis tumida is measured. I dropped the year and the word "report", and left out the phototaxis claim because the R2 value text is cut off.

input.text: If you are a Dampier's fiddler crab, your eyes are far more sensitive at night, and the dimmest flash that gives an electrical signal from your eye is about a thousand times dimmer than the one needed by day. Nobody has measured how dim a light you can see if you are most other crabs, crayfish or shrimp.
input.note: Left out R2 and R3: their figures are calculated from eye dimensions in other species, and numbers do not travel.

input.text: A human reads about 30 cycles a degree on an eye chart, and the sharks measured in these records see less fine detail than that. If you are a great white shark, the retinas of two young ones give a best case of about 5 cycles a degree, and a review lists 11 for the bigeye thresher and 2 for the brown-banded bamboo shark. For most other sharks and rays, nobody has measured how sharply you see.
input.note: Replaced "reports" with "lists" for the voice check. Left out Port Jackson, wobbegong, epaulette, skate and stingray figures to keep the row short; the row stays at i because most species are unmeasured.

input.text: Nobody has measured the color-sensing cells of a woodlouse. In the wharf roach, an isopod related to you that lives on shores, a compilation of measurements lists three kinds, and one of them senses ultraviolet light, which humans cannot see. Nobody knows whether you have the same three.
input.note: Left out the 340, 470 and 520 nm values because they belong to the wharf roach alone. R1 and R4 are lizard records and were not used.

input.text: Some fishes have a color-sensing cell tuned to ultraviolet, light that humans cannot see at all: a table in a review lists one in goldfish near 355 nanometers, and measurements found one near 365 in zebrafish and in the damselfish Pomacentrus amboinensis. If you are any other fish, nobody has measured whether you have one, and for the western mosquitofish only a prediction from its gene sequence puts one near 355. Spadefish, tautog and black sea bass were tested only from 400 to 600 nanometers, a range that stops short of ultraviolet.
input.note: Goldfish figure comes from a compilation (R2, partial). Left out the bluegill/bass carry (R10) and carp (R17), since neither record gives an ultraviolet value. Reworded "reports" to pass the voice check.

input.text: Along each side of the front of your body sit several small eyes. A survey of 20 species in the family Buthidae, which includes the bark scorpions, found 5 pairs of these side eyes, where earlier works had counted only 3 pairs. Nobody has measured how many side eyes you have in your own species, so that count is still unknown.
input.note: R1 is a family-level survey that does not name the species counted, so the count stays open for each listed species. I left out the specimen total and any claim about the median eyes, which no record covers.

input.text: You have no eyes, yet light matters to you, and nobody has measured how most slime molds sense it. If you are a dog vomit slime mold, a 1950 paper reviewing work from 1938 states that you cannot form fruiting bodies without light. If you are Physarum polycephalum, a light-sensing pigment called a phytochrome is one reason your plasmodium breaks into fragments in light, and if you are Didymium iridis, you need both starvation and light before you make spores.
input.note: Replaced "reports" with a description of the 1950 review; left out the 680 and 750 nm absorption peaks since they have no job for a reader.

input.text: A light that looks steady to one fish can look like it is flashing to another. In measurements compiled in reviews, the painted comber stops seeing flicker at about 25 flashes a second, the goldfish at about 65 and the flathead mullet at more than 100, where a human stops at about 60. Nobody has measured this in a bluegill, a bass or a carp, so nobody knows how fast you see.
input.note: Replaced "report" to satisfy the voice check. Left out the Atlantic salmon figure (R11) because numbers do not carry to brown trout.

input.text: Nobody has measured how fast a light can flash before you stop seeing it flicker, and that is true for most crabs. If you are a Dampier's fiddler crab, your eyes follow a flicker of about 75 flashes a second by day and about 60 at night, where a human stops at about 60. A review lists 14 flashes a second for the deep-sea crab Bathynectes longipes.
input.note: No flicker measurement exists in the records for the commonly met crabs, so the row names only two measured crabs.

input.text: A human reads about 30 cycles a degree on an eye chart, and owls range from far below that to a little above it. If you are a barn owl of the kind called Tyto alba pratincola, a compilation lists only 4, and a tawny owl tested on behavior reads about 11. Estimates from the density of cells in the retina give about 15 for a burrowing owl, 25 for a great gray owl, 30 for a great horned owl and 40 for a snowy owl.
input.note: Replaced "reports" with "lists" for the voice check. Used R1 (4) for barn owl and left out R5 (American barn owl, 13.6 by retinal estimate). Owls with no record (screech owls, saw-whet and others) are not covered.

input.text: A review describes very high numbers of touch-sensing units in the bill-tip organ of filter-feeding and dabbling ducks, so if you feed that way, the tip of your bill very likely holds many of them. Nobody has measured how sensitive the rest of your body is to touch.
input.note: R1 covers only filter-feeding and dabbling ducks, so geese, swans and other ducks get no claim. No record gives touch measurements for the rest of the body. Removed "reports" per the voice check.

input.text: Newts hunting prey against a gray card have shown that they see color. A review lists this for alpine, great crested and smooth newts, and fire salamander larvae can also tell colored light from white light. If you are any other salamander or newt, nobody has measured whether you see color.
input.note: R4 quote is cut off, so I left out the retina finding about blue-yellow cells. Replaced "reports" with "lists" to pass the voice check.

input.text: If you are a sand-dwelling scorpion, Paruroctonus mesaensis, slit-shaped sense organs on your legs respond to ripples in the sand made by insects up to 50 centimeters away, according to a paper's abstract. A review says the sensory hairs and trichobothria of scorpions react to air streams and are sensitive to the direction the air comes from. Nobody has measured either sense in most scorpions, so how far your own legs and hairs reach is unknown.
input.note: Left out R1, R2 and R5 (R1 and R2 are single-species behavior tests; R5 repeats R3). R3 is from an abstract and R4 from a review, so the row says so.

input.text: If you are a mallard, a table in a review of earlier measurements lists a violet-sensitive cone in your eye. Nobody has measured how many kinds of color-sensing cell you have. In the Nēnē, a Hawaiian goose, a study found a violet-sensitive cone as well, so a violet-sensitive cone may be common among ducks and geese, though for most of them nobody has measured it.
input.note: Replaced "reports" and dropped the nanometer figures because they had no comparison to do. R1's other columns are unlabeled and R2's value is cut off, so I left out the other cone peaks and the cone count.

input.text: If you are an African bush elephant, you see a little under half the fine detail a human sees. A calculation from how tightly the cells that carry signals out of your retina are packed puts your best sharpness at about 14 cycles a degree, where a human reads about 30 on an eye chart.
input.note: Removed the one-word label that was flagged as a fragment. The value is an anatomical estimate (13.16 to 14.37), so the row says it is calculated. No other elephant species has a record.

input.text: If you are a douroucouli, a review states that your eyes have only one kind of color-sensing cone, where a human has three. If you are an Azara's night monkey or a northern lesser galago, you very likely have just one kind as well, since a table lists one kind for owl monkeys and for galagos. Nobody has measured the color-sensing cells of the brown greater galago.
input.note: No record covers the brown greater galago or other monkeys and apes, so the row stays with night monkeys and galagos.

input.text: If you are a Pacific crown-of-thorns, the tiny units that make up each of your eyes point about 8 degrees apart. If you are a blue Linckia, they point about 16 degrees apart, which is twice as coarse. Juvenile Acanthaster measured about 17 degrees, and nobody has measured this in the purple starfish, the chocolate chip sea star or the Northern Pacific seastar.
input.note: No record states that the eyes sit at the arm tips, so the row leaves that to the title. Removed the word "reports" and the review credit, since R1 and R2 are not marked PARTIAL.

input.text: Your skin may sense light all over your body. If you are a greenhouse millipede, an experiment found that your skin senses light and that light changes how much you move, without steering you toward or away from it. Nobody has measured whether other millipedes sense light through the skin.
input.note: Removed the year. R1's quote says "both species" without naming the second, so I named only the greenhouse millipede. R1 does not say whether light speeds you up or slows you down, so I left that out.

input.text: If you are a Kuhl's pipistrelle, a calculation from your measured call levels puts the distance at which you can detect an insect at a few meters. For Eptesicus bottae, an open-air hunter, an estimate from field recordings gives about 20 meters for large objects. For most other bats, nobody has measured how far you can detect things.
input.note: Dropped the word "reports" and my unsupported opening line. R3's quote is cut off, so I used "a few meters" and left out the other threshold ranges. R8 is an estimate for Eptesicus bottae only.

input.text: Nobody has measured how sharply you see if you are a bear, a raccoon, a skunk or a hedgehog, and most other mammals in this group are unmeasured too. Where it has been measured, a wild boar and a western gray kangaroo each see about a third of the fine detail a human sees, and a koala sees about a twelfth. Those figures stay with those species.
input.note: Corrected "grey" to "gray". Kept to three measured species for brevity; the elephant, rhinoceros, hippopotamus and opossum values were left out.

input.text: Picture a plasmodium that has eaten everything around it and is running out of food. In two slime molds, Physarum polycephalum and Didymium iridis, starvation and light are both needed to trigger spore-making, and a review states that the dog vomit slime mold cannot fruit without light. Nobody has measured this in other slime molds, so if you are another species, nobody knows whether you need light to fruit.
input.note: Left out the year of the review, since no record quote states it. R1 (phytochrome in Physarum) concerns plasmodium fragmentation, not hunger, so I left it out.

input.text: An insect a few meters away is about as far as a Kuhl's pipistrelle can detect by echo, according to a calculation from its measured calls. A review gives an estimate of about 20 meters for large objects in Eptesicus bottae, a bat that hunts in open air. If you are another species, nobody has measured how far away you detect things by echo.
input.note: R3's value text (20 dB SPL) and its quote (the higher threshold) disagree, so I gave only "a few meters" (the quote spans 2 to 7 m for Kuhl's pipistrelle). The Eptesicus bottae figure is an estimate and stays with that species.

input.text: One pair of your eyes is easy to spot, and two more pairs are hidden. If you are a European harvestman, a review of gene-expression work found that one hidden pair is a lateral pair, shrunken and moved inside your body, and the other is an extra pair of median eyes that is just as cryptic.
input.note: R1 is an abstract and its value text is cut off, so the row gives no total count and says nothing about what the hidden eyes sense.

input.text: One millipede, Paraspirobolus lucifugus, moves away from light and is active only at night, and its daily rhythm is apparently run by an internal clock, according to the abstract of a 2022 paper by Meyer-Rochow. Nobody has recorded whether you are active at night or by day.
input.note: Only one record, from an abstract about one species; nothing on the listed species, so the row stays grade i. Replaced "reports" to pass the voice check.

input.text: Nobody has measured whether you sense red light. In the red bread mold, light works best at starting carotenoid pigment production when it is blue, and a review of the pin mold Phycomyces found that it bends toward blue light most strongly as well.
input.note: No record tests red light on these species, so the row says red is unmeasured and names the two molds that peak in blue. Wavelength numbers left out because they do no comparing.

input.text: A review states that in land snails and slugs the optics cannot produce a focused image on the shallow retina, so if you are one, you very likely see no sharp image. If you are a periwinkle, the same kind of review states that the lens of Littorina forms a sharp image on the retina, and if you are a nudibranch, a natural history account says your small eyes sit deep inside your body and tell light from dark without seeing images. Nobody has counted how many eyes you have.
input.note: No record gives an eye count for any species, so the count is stated as unknown.

input.text: If you are the sea slug Berghia stephanieae, you go straight to a black stripe set outside the arena where you are placed. A meeting abstract describes this test and says you did it reliably.
input.note: R1's value is cut off at a second stripe test ("isolumin..."), and the quote does not state it, so I left it out. I also left out other sea slugs, since no record covers them. I replaced "reports" because of the voice check.

input.text: If you are a cheetah, a compilation of published values lists your eyesight at about 25 cycles a degree, a little below the 30 a human reads on an eye chart. Nobody has measured how sharply you see if you are a lion, tiger, leopard, jaguar or any other big cat. A textbook survey says only that the great cats have high visual acuity, and it gives no measurement.
input.note: Cheetah value is a compiled figure with no method stated, rounded to about 25. The house cat figure (R1) was left out because acuity numbers do not travel across genera. The textbook year was dropped because it is not in the record.

input.text: A human reads about 30 cycles a degree on an eye chart, and you see much less fine detail than that. If you are a black, gray-headed or little red flying fox, counts of nerve cells in your eye put your sharpness at between 4 and 6 cycles a degree, a fifth of a human's or less. If you are a Madagascan rousette, the estimate is about 3, roughly a tenth of a human's.
input.note: Gray-headed has two figures (about 4 in R1, 5.5 in R3), so I gave a 4 to 6 range. I left out the Egyptian rousette, because R1 lists it but its quote does not state a value for it.

input.text: Ultraviolet is light that humans cannot see at all. In eight bat species, pigments made in a lab for the ultraviolet-sensing cell peak at about 360 nanometers, and a review lists the same peak, predicted from its gene, for the flying fox Pteropus samoensis. You very likely have this pigment too, but nobody has measured how far into the ultraviolet you see.
input.note: R1 does not name its eight species, so I could not say whether any is a flying fox. R2 is a gene-based prediction. No record gives a spectral range.

input.text: Many harvestmen, but not all, have a pair of eyes with a lens in the hard outer layer of the body, set on a small tower in the middle of the back. If you are a European harvestman, the abstract of a review of gene-expression work describes that visible pair, plus a hidden inner pair of side eyes and a second hidden pair of median eyes. For other harvestmen nobody has recorded how many eyes you have or what kind they are, and nobody has measured how well you see.
input.note: R1's value is cut off, so I used only the pairs its quote and value name. I did not total the eyes.

input.text: If you are a European common cuttlefish, your eyes have only one visual pigment, and a paper reports that cuttlefish have been shown to be color blind. A review lists one pigment for the common octopus as well, and three for the firefly squid. For most other octopuses, squid and cuttlefish, nobody has measured how many kinds of color-sensing cell you have.
input.note: Dropped the year, and left out peak wavelengths (480 to 540 nm) because they have no job here and differ by species.

input.text: If you are a lone star tick, an abstract of an electron microscope study describes your eye as one lens of cuticle over 30 to 40 light-sensing nerve cells. If you belong to another Amblyomma species, you very likely have the same kind of eye, since the lone star tick does. If you belong to any other kind of tick, nobody has recorded what your eye is made of.
input.note: R1 is an abstract, so the row gives only the lens and the 30 to 40 cells. The pore canals are left out, and the year is left out because no record states it.

input.text: You live underground, where a commentary on the maritime centipede's genome says every centipede in your order, the Geophilomorpha, is blind. Nobody has reported an eye count for your own species, so nobody can say for certain that you have no eyes.
input.note: R1 is a commentary stating that all Geophilomorpha are blind, but no record gives an eye count for these species, so the row stays at grade i.

input.text: For most fish, nobody has measured where the sharpest part of the retina lies, so for most of you nobody knows where yours is. A white crappie has its most densely packed cone cells in the part of its retina that looks forward, a golden shiner has a sharp patch of its own, a black-faced blenny has a pit called a fovea in the upper part of its retina, and a zebra danio larva has a patch of ultraviolet-sensing cells aimed at the upper front, where ultraviolet-bright prey swim. A review describes a vertical streak in the glyrna.
input.note: Left out cone densities, the black crappie (carried from the white crappie only) and the frogfish streak (R6, not a listed relative).

input.text: Picture a mole digging through the soil close to you. Nobody has measured whether you sense the shaking of that digging. The closest measurement is in the Mediterranean medicinal leech, where an abstract of nerve recordings proposes that a cell called the S cell detects water waves.
input.note: Left out R2: its quote reports fewer earthworms near wind turbines, which does not state that earthworms sense vibration.

input.text: Monkeys and apes differ in how many kinds of color-sensing cell they have, and for most of you nobody has measured it. If you are a crab-eating macaque, your three kinds peak near 430, 530 and 560 nanometers, and a table in a review lists three kinds in macaques generally, so other macaques very likely have three as well. Howler monkeys have three in males and females alike, so a howler very likely has three, while the same review lists squirrel monkeys with two kinds, or three in some females, and ring-tailed lemurs have two.
input.note: Reworded "reports" to "lists" to pass the voice check. Left out the human peak numbers (R1) for monkeys, since they cannot carry over. Baboons, vervets, capuchins, spider monkeys and marmosets are covered only by the opening sentence.

input.text: If you are a green shore crab, a review lists your sharpness at about half a cycle a degree, a sixtieth of the 30 cycles a degree a human reads on an eye chart. If you are a horned ghost crab, the same review lists under 2 cycles a degree, about a twentieth of a human's. Nobody has measured how sharply you see if you are a Dungeness crab, a Sally Lightfoot crab or a northern kelp crab, among many others.
input.note: Left out the blue crab's 1.8 degree figure (R30) because it is an angle, and no record converts it to cycles a degree. Rounded the horned ghost crab's 1.57 to "under 2".

input.text: If you are a goldfish, a table of fish eyes lists four kinds of color-sensing cell for you, where a human has three, and a review states four for rainbow trout as well. If you are a Florida largemouth bass, you have two kinds, and a study of your eye found no evidence of a cell for short wavelengths. For most other fish nobody has measured how many kinds you have, so nobody knows how your colors compare with a human's.
input.note: Replaced "report" with "lists" and "states". Left out wavelength peaks (R3, R13, R15 to R19, R22) because they belong to single species and have no job in a row for all fish.

input.text: A review states that, based on physiological evidence, scorpions can apparently see 360 degrees around their bodies, a full circle. Nobody has measured how far around you your own eyes see.
input.note: R1 is a review's statement about scorpions as a group, so I kept it as a statement from a review and said it is unmeasured in your species.

input.text: Nobody has measured how wide an area you take in at once, or how much of it both of your eyes see together. Both have been measured in the domestic cat, which belongs to a different genus, and those figures cannot be carried over to you.
input.note: I left out all numbers. The two domestic cat records disagree on overlap (R1 implies about 60 degrees, R2 gives 140), and no record covers any big cat.

input.text: If you are a Caribbean reef octopus, you can see a light flicker at up to about 70 flashes a second in very bright light, a little above the human limit of about 60, and the same figure was measured in the common octopus. If you are a bigfin reef squid, your limit is about 50, and if you are a European common cuttlefish, it is below 30. Nobody has measured it in most other octopuses, squid and cuttlefish, including the giant Pacific octopus and the California market squid.
input.note: Reworded to drop "reports". Kept to measured species because the row grade is i; the cuttlefish record gives only "<30" and the octopus figure was taken at very high light intensity.

input.text: If you are a European medicinal leech, the touch-sensing cells in your body wall respond to stimulation repeated up to about 50 to 60 times a second, according to an abstract of an electrophysiology study. Nobody has measured how touch works in the other worms and leeches, so for them it is unknown.
input.note: Only touch is supported; no records for taste or damp, so they are left out despite the title. Removed the year because it is not in the record.

input.text: A human reads about 30 cycles a degree on an eye chart, and a compilation of bird eyes lists about 12 for the mallard, estimated from how densely nerve cells are packed in its retina. If you are a mallard, you see about two fifths of the fine detail a human sees, and if you are a Canada goose, about a third. The same compilation gives about 11 for the lesser scaup, the greater scaup and the northern shoveler.
input.note: Figures are anatomical estimates from a compilation (Caves 2024). Other ducks are not measured or are only carried from relatives, so they are left out.

input.text: If you are a meadow mushroom and your cap is tilted by up to 30 degrees, your gills turn back to straight down, and if you are a splitgill mushroom, your gills develop facing down in response to gravity. A review of experiments on gilled mushrooms found that their stems grow away from gravity and their gills grow toward it. Nobody has measured whether most other fungi sense which way is down.
input.note: Left out R3 (Coprinopsis cinerea, not on the species list). No record covers lichens, so the row does not mention them. Replaced "reports" with "found" because the voice check rejects it.

input.text: If you are an Androctonus australis, your two median eyes are about 1,000 times more sensitive to light at night than by day, and this daily rhythm keeps going even in constant darkness. A review of scorpion eyes says the median eyes of some desert scorpions may see well enough to use the horizon for orientation, even on moonless nights. For every other scorpion, nobody has measured how little light your eyes need.
input.note: Replaced "reports" with "says". Left out the review's pigment-migration claim because its quote does not state it. Only Androctonus australis is measured.

input.text: If you are a European common cuttlefish, a review describes your pupil as a horizontal slit shaped like a W in bright light, and as a circle in darkness. Nobody has measured the pupil of the other octopuses, squid and cuttlefish, so if you are one of them, the shape of your pupil is unknown.
input.note: Only Sepia officinalis has a record, and it is partial (a review), so the shape is not carried to other cuttlefish. Replaced "reports" with "describes" to pass the voice check.

input.text: If you are an adult female lone star tick, at least 7 in 10 of your kind can detect a warm plate the size of a hand from a meter away. If you are an American dog tick, a review of the work states that unfed adults with their Haller's organs present move toward infrared light. Nobody has measured whether other ticks sense heat in this way.
input.note: Dropped the word "reports" per the voice check. Left out the 37 to 40 °C plate temperature and any organ-removal result, since R2's quote only states the result with organs present.

input.text: A review states that owls have outer ears hidden beneath the feathers of the facial disc, and that some species can hunt by hearing alone. If you are a barn owl, your best hearing is about 20 decibels more sensitive than that of other birds, and if you are a great gray owl, you can plunge through snow onto prey without seeing it. Nobody has measured how well most other owls hear.
input.note: Hearing is measured only in the barn owl and the great gray owl, so the barn owl figure stays with that species. I replaced "reports" with "states" to pass the voice check.

input.text: If you are a common octopus, the light-sensing tubes in neighboring cells of your eye lie at right angles to each other, which most likely lets you sense polarized light. If you are a day octopus, you notice a change of about 1 degree in the angle of polarized light, ten times finer than a crayfish does. Nobody has measured whether a squid senses polarized light.
input.note: Dropped the cuttlefish caustics claim (R4) because that record covers both a cuttlefish and a crab and its quote does not name the species. Left out R3 and R5 for length.

input.text: A human reads about 30 cycles a degree on an eye chart, and the few reef fish that have been measured read far fewer. If you are a black-faced blenny, the spacing of the cells in your eye gives 7 to 9, and if you are an Ambon damselfish, a test with striped patterns gave a little over 1. A compilation of earlier measurements lists about 3 for the lagoon triggerfish, 7 for the Koran angelfish and 14 for the red grouper, and nobody has measured most other reef fish.
input.note: Replaced "reports" with "lists". Left out R4 (quote gives no value) and R2 (freshwater bass, value and quote disagree). Carried grades are not stated, since figures stay with the measured species.

input.text: Nobody has measured how sharply you see. Of the isopods, only one has been measured: if you are a Natatolana borealis, a review table reports that your compound eye reads less than a hundredth of the fine detail a human reads.
input.note: Dropped the decimal 0.05 and gave it as a comparison with a human's 30 cycles a degree. Left out R3 (Cirolana), whose quote does not state the 0.033 value, and R2, which is a lizard.

input.text: If you are a castor bean tick, you have strings of light-sensing cells on your left and right sides, and a 2003 paper by Perret says they sense shifts in light intensity. Nobody has measured this in any other tick, so if you are another kind, nobody knows whether you have these strings or how well they work.
input.note: R1's quote does not state "no eyes", so I left that claim out. Only Ixodes ricinus has a record, and it was read from an abstract.

input.text: If you are a common barn owl, a review states that your two eyes can turn toward each other by no more than 4 degrees, where a human's can turn up to 30 degrees. If you are a tawny owl, eye movements were absent or not readily produced by the methods used to look for them. Nobody has measured how the eyes of most other owls move.
input.note: R2's quote says "some species" without naming the tawny owl, so the tawny owl wording rests on the record's taxon. R3 (head-bobbing) left out because it is not about eye movement.

input.text: If you are a bigfin reef squid, your two eyes together cover about 320 degrees, almost a full circle, and you very likely have a similar field if you are another Sepioteuthis reef squid. If you are the cuttlefish Sepia esculenta, both your eyes see the same area over about 85 degrees at the front, and you very likely have a similar overlap if you are another Sepia cuttlefish. If you are an octopus, nobody has measured how wide your field is, and a review states that some researchers dispute that your two eyes overlap at all.
input.note: Left out R3: its 177 degrees for the European common cuttlefish is an old estimate that model calculations say is far too large, so no value is stated. Dropped the squid age to avoid an unrounded number.
